subject: ba
title: Business Analysis and Evaluation Tools
objectives: Define business analysis and explain its importance.
Describe the steps and distinguish the types of business analysis (strategic, tactical, operational).
State the objectives and uses of business analysis.
Apply SWOT, PEST(LE), MOST and CATWOE as evaluation tools.
Conduct basic financial analysis using liquidity, profitability and solvency ratios.
Draw and interpret a Process Flow Diagram.
study:
Business analysis is a well-curated, actionable method of identifying business needs and finding solutions to business problems — anything from a software upgrade to a process improvement or a new policy. A Business Analyst is the person responsible for identifying and defining these problems to maximise organisational output, and typically operates across every level of the organisation.

Business analysis comes in three types. Strategic analysis is pre-project work — identifying business problems and devising strategies, goals and objectives for top management. Tactical analysis applies specific techniques at the right time within a given project. Operational analysis focuses on business improvement by leveraging information technology and studying existing systems for opportunities.

Key termSWOT Analysis — a subjective assessment of a business unit organised into Strengths and Weaknesses (internal factors) and Opportunities and Threats (external factors).

SWOT is best completed as a team, since perceptions from multiple people improve the quality of the output. It measures a specific business unit, whereas PEST(LE) analysis measures broader external trends — Political, Economic, Social, Technological (and often Legal and Environmental). It's common to run a PEST analysis before, alongside, or after a SWOT.

Exam tipKeep the internal/external split straight: SWOT's Strengths and Weaknesses are internal, Opportunities and Threats are external. PEST(LE) is entirely external/macro-environmental.

Financial analysis uses statements like the balance sheet and income statement to calculate ratios: liquidity ratios (ability to pay short-term debts), profitability ratios (efficiency in generating earnings/return), and solvency ratios.

MOST analysis checks internal strategic alignment across four levels: Mission (why the business exists), Objectives (specific goals), Strategy (the long-term plan to achieve those objectives), and Tactics (the short-term, day-to-day actions that execute the strategy).

CATWOE analysis defines the scope of a business process across six elements: Customers (who benefits), Actors (who does the work), Transformation (what the process actually does), Worldview (the bigger picture justifying it), Owner (who has the authority to stop or change the process), and Environmental constraints (the external limits on the system).

Finally, a Process Flow Diagram is a visual map of the sequential steps in a business process, commonly used to document a process, study it for improvement, and help stakeholders understand and communicate about operations — its main practical use is spotting bottlenecks and redundancies.
recap:
• Business analysis types: Strategic (pre-project, top management) · Tactical (technique at the right time) · Operational (IT-driven improvement).
  • SWOT: Strengths/Weaknesses = internal; Opportunities/Threats = external. Best done as a team.
  • PEST(LE): external/macro only — Political, Economic, Social, Technological (+Legal, Environmental).
  • Financial ratios: Liquidity (short-term debt) · Profitability (earnings efficiency) · Solvency.
  • MOST: Mission → Objectives → Strategy → Tactics.
  • CATWOE: Customers, Actors, Transformation, Worldview, Owner, Environmental constraints.
  • Process Flow Diagram: visual map used to spot bottlenecks and improve understanding.
